title: Teaching Robots to Feel: DAIMON's Massive Touch Dataset Aims to Transform Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Robots can see and hear, but they've largely been numb to the world — until now. DAIMON Robotics, a Hong Kong-based startup, has unveiled Daimon-Infinity, a colossal dataset designed to give robot hands a sense of touch. Described as the largest omni-modal dataset for physical AI, it integrates high-resolution tactile sensing with vision, motion, and language across a vast range of tasks, from folding laundry to assembly-line manufacturing. At the heart of this initiative is DAIMON's advanced tactile sensor, a fingertip-sized module that packs over 110,000 effective sensing units. Unlike basic pressure sensors, this vision-based device captures deformation, slip, friction, material properties, and surface textures, enabling a comprehensive reconstruction of physical interactions. "Data scarcity remains a primary bottleneck in robot learning, particularly the lack of physical interaction data," said Prof. Michael Yu Wang, DAIMON's co-founder and chief scientist. To address this, the company built a distributed data-collection network that can generate millions of hours of data annually. They've open-sourced 10,000 hours of it to accelerate research. The dataset was developed with partners including Google DeepMind, Northwestern University, and the National University of Singapore. It spans over 80 real-world scenarios and 2,000 human-demonstrated skills, making it a rich resource for training general-purpose robotic foundation models. Prof. Wang, a pioneer in the field, advocates for a Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) architecture, elevating touch to a modality on par with vision. "Our goal is to provide the high-quality 'fuel' needed to power embodied AI," he said. With this dataset, robots could soon perform delicate tasks that require a nuanced sense of touch — from handling fragile items in warehouses to assisting in surgery. DAIMON envisions early deployments in hotels and convenience stores across China, where touch-enabled robots might soon handle everyday objects with human-like dexterity.
why_it_matters: As robots move from factory cages into everyday human spaces, a refined sense of touch is what will stop accidents, enable delicate tasks, and make them genuinely useful; this dataset could fast-track that leap, influencing everything from healthcare to retail — and shaping how future generations interact with machines.

background_read: While robots have gained vision through cameras and speech through microphones, creating a high-resolution sense of touch has been a hard challenge because it requires sensors that can detect tiny forces, vibrations, and textures.

Prof. Michael Yu Wang, co-founder of Hong Kong-based DAIMON Robotics (a special administrative region of China known for its tech startup ecosystem), previously pioneered vision-based tactile sensors that use cameras inside a silicone finger to see deformation.

Major AI labs like Google DeepMind (the company behind AlphaGo and Gemini) and universities such as Northwestern University (a leading US institution in robotics) and the National University of Singapore have joined this project, reflecting a global race to build ‘foundation models’ for physical robots just as GPT models transformed language.

Data scarcity in physical interaction has long bottlenecked robot learning; open-sourcing 10,000 hours of omni-modal data aims to replicate the impact that ImageNet had on computer vision by giving researchers a massive, standardized touch dataset.

The vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) architecture treats touch as a core sense, not an add-on, which could allow robots to handle everything from raw eggs to surgical tools with human-like dexterity.

perspectives.description: Giving robots a rich touch sense could massively improve tasks like handling fragile items, folding laundry, or assisting surgeons, reducing costs and errors in logistics and medicine.

Highly capable touch-enabled robots might accelerate job displacement in warehouses and service industries; moreover, giving physical robots such nuanced sensing raises new safety questions if systems malfunction in close human proximity.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — Following a well-known data playbook
perspectives.description: The project mirrors how ImageNet transformed computer vision; open-sourcing a huge labeled dataset may similarly catalyze touch robotics. However, real-world tactile data is much harder to standardize and collect, so success is not guaranteed.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — Need for regulation and standards
perspectives.description: As touch-enabled robots enter hotels and stores, policymakers will need to define safety benchmarks, liability frameworks, and privacy rules, especially since tactile sensors could capture detailed information about objects and environments.
